During the discussion we note that putting these questions in just this way reflects a peculiar affront to the practice of deductive thinking
Subse- quently, we ask if anyone can explain the fallacy indicated by this particular line of questioning

With little further provocation the students quickly point out that given the word freedom means absence of restraint, then, if there is to be an absence of restraint upon a per- son's speech then a person must, logi- cally speaking, be free to shout Fire or any other such thing when and where they choose
Logically speaking one cannot aver that there must be freedom of speech and then proceed to list pro- hibitions against it
At this point we find we ask the chil- dren what the point is to having a con- stitutional provision regarding our acts of speech
Without fail the children quickly begin by noting that it would be imprudent to create a license to speak so unbridled that the welfare of others may be directly imperiled as a result
Instead, they conclude that the point behind such a constitutional provision is to create a right which de- limits the restraints that might be im- posed on a given speaker or a given set of ideas
Thus, a discussion about con- stitutional protections becomes a les- son in logical analysis and a lesson in logical analysis illustrates the point behind initiating certain constitutional provisions

The children can now ad- dress directly the positive concern about which specific speech activities it is important to protect and how should a constitutional provision be interpreted so as to guarantee their protection
Such discussions are far less ani- mated than those which typically attempt to detail the rationale behind our constitutional protections

Nevertheless, we have found that chil- dren are intensely interested in both the process and outcome of such dis- cussions and, more importantly per- haps, they learn the extent to which skills of logical analysis can be em- ployed to make progress in under- standing an abstract issue of imme- diate social import
There is no area of the gifted student curriculum that cannot be similarly enhanced by supplementing traditional instruction with training in formal logic

For example, in the sciences theteacher can draw the student's atten- tion to a basic assumption regarding the reoccurrance of a particular phe- nomenon: There exists a field of attrac- tion between any two bodies

The teacher can then explain that even though every test of a hypothesis takes the form of a deductive (i.e., truth- guaranteeing) argument the assump- tions which initiate the hypothetical explanation must be the product of some prior conjecture on the part of a scientist
The children are then asked to consider the events that lead a scien- tist to make the assumptions that he or she makes
Typically, assumptions such as the law of gravity have been well confirmed by the scientists' experiences

But no scientist can have experiences of what will happen to- morrow (or at any other point in space- time with which he is unfamiliar) so generalized statements such as the law of gravity must be the product of an inductive inference
Subsequent to such discussion, students quickly be- gin to understand that both induction and deduction are necessary elements at different stages in the practice of experimental science

They recognize that the certainty which seems to accompany scientific conclusions is largely the result of the deductive form of argument characteristic of reports of the consequences of experimental research

Similarly, they recognize that the reason all scientific conclu- sions must be held tentatively is that the assumptions of science are the product of inductive thinking and as such necessarily contain an element of uncertainty

Conclusion Clearly, there is much to be gained in every area of the gifted curriculum by employing the definitions of deductive and inductive inference-making char- acteristic of the most recent advances in logic

In the face of such evidence it would be inexcusable to continue to fetter the child's understanding of inference-making by employing the Aristotelian definitions of deduction and induction that were so common in this country 50 years ago
As the for- mal study of logic advances so too must our understanding of its role in pedagogy
Alexander This article describes a training program in analogical reasoning skills based on Sternberg's componential processes research
Studentsare first taught how to apply the processes of encoding, inferring, mapping and applying in the solution of linguistic and nonlinguistic analogies of the A:B::C:D type
Then, they apply these components in the processing of extended linguistic analogies developed in sentence, paragraph, and story form
Finally, several weeks are spent teaching students the utility of these same components and analogical reasoning to their performance in the content areas
Patricia Alexander is assistant professor, teaching graduate courses in the areas of gifted and reading, at Texas A &M Uni- versity

The ultimate measure of any pro- gram should be its ability to deliver effective instruction to those learners it is intended to serve

struction is an active process that in- volves calculated models, suggestions, rules or injunctions that have a known influence on the way a child thinks rel- ative to some specific task (Belmont & Butterfield, 1977,p
One instruc- tional focus gaining favor in gifted programs is the training of intellectual skills
Following a quiescent period, there is now a burgeoning of programs aimed at enhancing the reasoning abil- ities of learners (Sternberg, 1983)
In describing the elements of the training program in analogical reason- ing, each of these criteria will be addressed
The Theoretical Base There are few intellectual skills as pervasive in or as essential to one's existence as the ability to reason analogically
We reason analog- ically whenever we determine that some conceptual or perceptual expe- rience parallels another
The term, analogy, is applied to a wide range of cognitive activities
Broadly defined, it describes a general learning strategy whereby unfamiliar stimuli are intro- duced with some reference to the more familiar
Teachers frequently apply this strategy - prefacing a new lesson with a review of known, related knowl- edge (Hayes & Tierney, 1980; Tierney & Cunningham, 1980; Marr & Gormley, 1982)
At its most specific, analogy refers to a particular type of reasoning problem of the form, A:B::C:D

According to Sternberg (1977, 1980,1981,1982), perhaps the most influen- tial researcher of analogies, the ability to reason analogically is predicted up- on the learner's ability to perform the component processes of encoding, in- ferring, mapping, and applying
These components represent the fundamen- tal units of processing, responsible for what is called intelligent behavior (Sternberg, 1977,p

Simply trans- lated, these components involve the following actions: Encoding - The attribute identifica- tion component; the representation of identifiable characteristics of each term in the analogy
The term, ball, for example, could be described by such attributes as round or bouncy
In the analogy, feather:bird::leaf:tree, the re- lationship between feather and bird is that feather is part of a bird (feather grows on bird)
In the analogy, king:prince::queen:prin- cess, king and queen are both members of royalty differentiated on the basis of gender
Applying - The completion of the analogy; the utilization of derived rules to generate the predicted response term
In the analogy, bat:ball::hammer: , the best answer would be nail since bat is used to hit a ball and a hammer is used to hit a nail
It is these empirically-tested compo- nent processes that will form the basis of this training program in analogical reasoning
Explicit Instruction As noted, effective instruction requires the appropriate trans- lation of theory into explicit in- structional content
Therefore, while the component processes of analogical reasoning serve as the content of in- struction, the principles of direct in- struction structure the delivery of that content

According to the principles of direct instruction, the training program is teacher-directed; that is, the presen- tation and pacing of the lessons are under the instructor's control (Duffy, 1981; Rosenshine, 1979)

Toward this end, a three-day initial training phase was prepared in scripted form.* By scripting the initial phase of training, there can be adequate guidance to the teacher, as well as some control for in- formation presentation

Another principle of direct instruc- tion includes extensive coverage of *The script of the initial training phase is available upon request from the author.content, sequenced from simple to com- plex
For this purpose, Session One of the training moves from instruction in nonlinguistic, concrete analogies to non- linguistic, abstract analogies, both of the A:B::C:D format

The concrete, non- linguistic analogy problems are simple drawings of familiar objects (ex., ^ : JS " 0 : $ ), while abstract, non- linguistic problems consist of geomet- ric figures (ex., A : • ::O : • )• Within each set, concrete and abstract, there is an attempt to move from easier to more difficult problems

Those applying this type of train- ing program must take care that the selection of sample prob- lems, and the pacing of material be de- termined by the abilities, interests, and maturity of the learners involved
While commercial materials may be available for use in the training, espe- cially with older learners, the author has found it advisable to generate prac- tice problems
Analogy problems can be easily developed using available classroom materials (ex., pictures, drawing from unused readers, work- books)
Older students and parents can assist in the development of training materials

Test materials, such as the Lorge-Thorndike Intelligence Tests (Lorge, Thorndike & Hagen, 1964) and the Cognitive Abilities Test (Thorn- dike & Hagen, 1978), serve as ready sources of model analogy problems
In Session One, instruction begins with an explanation to the students of training goals, and a definition of anal- ogy
Students are told that analogies are a special type of reasoning problem that can be solved by following spe- cific steps
At this point, the compo- nent processes are introduced and de- scribed

Once students demonstrate un- derstanding of the components, this knowledge is applied, first, to a series of concrete, nonlinguistic analogy prob- lems, and, then, to a series of abstract, nonlinguistic analogy problems
The first session is structured to provide group practice, followed by independ- ent practice
Another principle of direct instruc- tion specifies that students' progress should be monitored and instruction appropriately adapted
In addition, feedback to the student should be im- mediate and academically-oriented (Duffy, 1981; Rosenshine, 1979; Sam- uels, 1981)
These principles, as well, have been incorporated in the analogi- cal reasoning training program
